## 1. The problem

### 1.1 What a programmer sees today

Register the ordinary thing:

```clojure
(rf/reg-event :order/submit
  (fn [{:keys [db]} _]
    {:fx [[:rf.http/managed {:request    {:method :post :url "/api/checkout/finalize"
                                          :body   {:cart-id (:cart-id db)}}
                             :request-id :checkout
                             :reply-to   [:checkout/done]}]]}))
```

Open the `:order/submit` epoch in Xray. The managed-fx record reads (`tools/xray/src/day8/re_frame2_xray/panels/managed_fx_template.cljs:31-39`, the ns docstring's own picture):

```
┌─ MANAGED FX [HTTP] · :rf.http/managed ────────────────────────┐
│ STATUS: ◦ ISSUED · correlation: :checkout                      │
│ ▶ REQUEST                                                      │
│ ▶ REPLY TARGET                                                 │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

That is true, and it is all the record can say: `http-adapter` sets `:phase`, `:wire`, `:res`, `:duration-ms`, `:http-status` to nil "BY CONSTRUCTION rather than pending" (`managed_fx_helpers.cljc:661-714`). The record reads `ERROR` only for a failure the issuing bundle itself witnessed — a synchronous body-prep failure, or (CLJS) an already-aborted `:abort-signal` (`managed_fx_helpers.cljc:604-659`, rf2-n3sx9).

Whether the request succeeded, failed with a 500, timed out, retried, or was cancelled is not on the record. To find out, the programmer has to locate the **reply-dispatch bundle** — the later `[:checkout/done {:status :ok …}]` event, dispatched with `:source :http` (`implementation/http/src/re_frame/http/encoding.cljc:322`) — and read the reply map off its event args. With a `:request-id`, the correlation pill's right-click filters the L2 list to exactly the issuing and reply-dispatch bundles (rf2-st7j0, PR #10010, merged 2026-09-18). **Without one there is no pill at all** — `args-correlation-id` returns `(:request-id args)` for `:http` (`managed_fx_helpers.cljc`, `args-correlation-id`), so an anonymous request gets no correlation and no right-click. The Resources panel does not help either: its stale-races section renders only arcs that were stale-SUPPRESSED (`resources.cljs:567-570`, `(filter :suppressed?)`), and its live-work section needs a work-ledger row that a plain managed request never has (`registry.cljc:887-889`: "a plain managed request has no ledger gate").

### 1.2 Why the completion cannot land in the issuing bundle

`emit!` and `emit-error!` build every trace row through `build-event`, which takes the run's dispatch-id from the dynamic `*handler-scope*` (`implementation/core/src/re_frame/trace.cljc:673-675`, `:706-708`). The grouper files any row with no `:rf.trace/dispatch-id` under `[nil :ungrouped]` (`implementation/core/src/re_frame/trace/projection.cljc:142-159`, `:189-199`). Every HTTP row after issuance is emitted either from the transport callback with no scope, or inside a DIFFERENT run's drain:

| op | emitted at | scope it inherits | lands in |
|---|---|---|---|
| `:rf.fx/handled` (the only issue-side row; tags `:rf.fx/id :rf.fx/args :frame`) | `implementation/core/src/re_frame/fx.cljc:1273-1278`, after the fx handler returns | the issuing run's | the issuing bundle's `:effects` |
| `:rf.http/replied` (tags = `trace-summary`: `:status`, `:rf.reply/work-id`, `:rf.reply/work-kind`, `:rf.reply/work-status`, `:attempt`, `:rf.frame/id`, `:completed-at`; `:value`/`:error`/`:correlation`/`:meta` elided) | `transport.cljc:557` — "OUTSIDE any `with-frame` scope" (`:538-541`) | none | `[nil :ungrouped]` |
| failure kinds `:rf.http/transport` / `timeout` / `http-4xx` / … (op-type `:error`, `:work/id` stamped by `self-identify`) | `transport.cljc:919` `(emit-error! (:kind failure) redacted)` | none (except the sync body-prep case) | ungrouped |
| `:rf.http/aborted` (`:work/id` via `self-identify`, `:reason`) | `transport.cljc:775` | the ABORTING run's, or none | another bundle or ungrouped |
| `:rf.http/retry-attempt` (`:request-id :url :attempt :max-attempts :failure :next-backoff-ms :recovery`) | `transport.cljc:1107` | none | ungrouped |
| `:rf.http/stale-suppressed` (`:rf.reply/work-id`, carried/current) | `transport.cljc:622`, `:705`; `registry.cljc:927` | the superseding run's, or none | the superseder's bundle or ungrouped |
| `:rf.http/aborted-on-actor-destroy` (`:request-id :actor-id :url` only) | `registry.cljc:869` | the destroying run's | the destroyer's bundle |

So the join must read the whole buffer (`[:rf.xray/trace-buffer]`), exactly as the Resources composite already does (`resources.cljs:1449`, `:1457`, `:1487`).

### 1.3 The join key, and where it is exact today

Every post-issuance row carries a work-id: `[:rf.work/http logical-id issuance attempt]` (`implementation/http/src/re_frame/http/reply.cljc:84-98`), where `logical-id` is the caller's `:request-id` when supplied, else the originating event-id; `issuance` is a monotonic per-(frame, request-id) counter allocated in the fx handler BEFORE superseding (`handlers.cljc:453`, `registry.cljc:516-527`); `attempt` is the retry number. The counter is evicted when the attempt terminates (`registry.cljc:502-514`), so a work-id is unique among LIVE work, not across the buffer — but a later re-issuance can only restart at 1 after the earlier attempt's completion row is already emitted, so key + time order is exact for any request that carries a `:request-id`.

The issue side carries none of this. `:rf.fx/handled`'s `:rf.fx/args` is the caller's raw map — `:request-id` if supplied, never the issuance number. So the only thing the two ends share today is `logical-id`, and the bead's join is "same logical-id, first completion after the issue time".

### 1.4 The finding the bead has backwards: the ambiguous case is the common case

`next-issuance!` returns **1 for every anonymous request** (`registry.cljc:524-525`: "Returns 1 for a nil `request-id` (an anonymous request never supersedes — there is nothing to discriminate)"). Two consequences:

- Two anonymous requests issued from one run of `[:search/go …]` carry the IDENTICAL work-id `[:rf.work/http :search/go 1 1]`. Nothing in the trace — not the work-id, not the completion row, not the Resources panel — can tell their completions apart. `spec/Managed-Effects.md:183` asks a work-id to be "frame-scoped enough to avoid intra-frame collision"; this is an intra-frame collision.
- Two OVERLAPPING runs of the same anonymous event (search-as-you-type with no `:request-id`, the debounce shape) also share it. Replies can arrive out of issue order, so "first completion after issue time" attributes the wrong reply.

How common is the anonymous shape? A bracket-matched census over every `[:rf.http/managed {…}]` form in the teaching corpus: **102 of 123 call sites (83%) carry no `:request-id`** — `examples/` 31 of 45, `docs/` 69 of 74 (control: the same census over `implementation/http/test` reads 132 of 201). So the bead's "ambiguous under precisely the storm cases the persona hunts" is inverted at source: the join is exact for the 17% that name their request and ambiguous by construction for the rest.

### 1.5 The other premises, checked at source

- **Clocks.** Correct that `:completed-at` is epoch ms (`interop.cljs:181-189`, `transport.cljc:354-377`) and trace `:time` is `performance.now()` (`interop.cljs:170-179`). But `build-event` stamps `:time` on EVERY row on that one clock (`trace.cljc:713`), so `duration = (:time replied-row) − (:time issue-row)` needs no second clock. A design slip in the original A, not a blocker.
- **"Spec 009 catalogue change, HOT-ZONE."** `:rf.http/replied` — the canonical completion row — has **0** rows in `spec/009-Instrumentation.md` (control: `:rf.http/retry-attempt` 6, catalogued at `:2292`); it is documented in `spec/014-HTTPRequests.md` prose (`:579-583`) and `Managed-Effects.md` §Tracing. So by precedent a new HTTP row lands in 014 + Managed-Effects (neither hot-zone); a 009 row is tidiness, sequenced if wanted.
- **"Fix the `:http-correlation` filter first."** Done: rf2-st7j0 closed 2026-09-17T22:42Z, PR #10010. Its finding matters here: the exchange's issuing and reply-dispatch bundles ARE identifiable without any producer change — but only through `:request-id`, which is why the anonymous case stays dark.
- **Supersession.** rf2-n3sx9 (PR #9952) fixed the record reddening on a healthy replacement request; the residue it named — an explicit `[:rf.http/managed-abort :x]` beside a same-id re-issue in one bundle is byte-identical to the already-aborted-signal case — is exactly a case the work-id resolves (the abort row carries the SUPERSEDED attempt's `:work/id`; the issue row, once it exists, carries the superseder's).
- **Managed-Effects §Tracing already requires an issuance row.** `spec/Managed-Effects.md:234`: families "MUST emit trace rows from the reply-envelope facts … issuance/start (with `:work/id`, frame, owner/cause, target summary), retries…, completion…, stale suppression…". Resources emit `:rf.resource/work-started {… :work/id work-id …}` inside the issuing handler (`implementation/resources/src/re_frame/resources/events.cljc:837-841`); mutations emit `:rf.mutation/started`; Xray's op→phase table lists both under `:issued` and records HTTP as the family with none — "HTTP issues the request through the `:rf.http/managed` fx; the canonical completion is `:rf.http/replied`" (`reply_envelope.cljc:389-398`). HTTP is the one family for which the generic `:rf.fx/handled` stands in for the spec'd issuance row.

### 1.6 What the ISSUED-only state costs the programmer

For the ordinary anonymous request: the record says the request went out; to learn whether it came back they scroll the L2 list for a `:source :http` event and read a reply map — with nothing linking the two bundles either way (`:rf.trace/parent-dispatch-id` is read off `*handler-scope*` at dispatch time, `router.cljc:235-236`, and a transport-callback dispatch has none, so the causality graph draws no edge). For a request that never came back (a timeout still retrying, an abort), there is no reply-dispatch bundle to find at all. The Xray spec calls the wire-boundary record "the single biggest 'I get re-frame2 now' win for new authors" (`tools/xray/spec/019-Cross-Cutting-Insight.md:654-657`); today its status line is a pill that says "sent".

## 2. Make it tangible

Three scenarios, what the trace holds, and what the record reads today versus under the join.

**(a) Search box, no `:request-id` — the common shape.** `[:search/go "re"]` then `[:search/go "ref"]` 80 ms later; the first reply lands after the second.

```
bundle [:app/main #401]  (:search/go "re")     :effects [:rf.fx/handled {:rf.fx/id :rf.http/managed :rf.fx/args {…}}]
bundle [:app/main #402]  (:search/go "ref")    :effects [:rf.fx/handled {…}]
[nil :ungrouped]  {:operation :rf.http/replied :tags {:status :ok :rf.reply/work-id [:rf.work/http :search/go 1 1] :attempt 1 :completed-at 1781…}}   ; "ref"'s
[nil :ungrouped]  {:operation :rf.http/replied :tags {:status :ok :rf.reply/work-id [:rf.work/http :search/go 1 1] …}}                               ; "re"'s
bundle [:app/main #403]  ([:search/results {:status :ok …}])   :source :http, no parent-dispatch-id
bundle [:app/main #404]  ([:search/results {:status :ok …}])
```

Today: both records read `◦ ISSUED`, no pill. Heuristic join: #401 takes the first completion after its time — "ref"'s — and both records now say `OK` with the wrong durations, silently. With the framework step (§4, option D): the two issue rows carry `[:rf.work/http :search/go 1 …]` and `[… 2 …]`, the completions carry the same, and each record reads its own `✓ OK 200 · 214ms` / `✓ OK 200 · 96ms`, with `→ reply ↗` focusing #404 / #403 exactly.

**(b) Checkout fails with a 500, retried once.** `:request-id :checkout`, `:retry {:on #{:rf.http/http-5xx} :max-attempts 2}`.

```
bundle [:app/main #347]   :effects [:rf.fx/handled {… :rf.fx/args {:request-id :checkout …}}]
[nil :ungrouped]  {:operation :rf.http/http-5xx      :op-type :error :tags {:kind :rf.http/http-5xx :status 500 :work/id [:rf.work/http :checkout 1 1] …}}
[nil :ungrouped]  {:operation :rf.http/retry-attempt :tags {:request-id :checkout :attempt 1 :next-backoff-ms 100 :recovery :retried}}
[nil :ungrouped]  {:operation :rf.http/http-5xx      :op-type :error :tags {… :work/id [:rf.work/http :checkout 1 2]}}
[nil :ungrouped]  {:operation :rf.http/replied       :tags {:status :error :rf.reply/work-id [:rf.work/http :checkout 1 2] :rf.reply/work-status :failed :attempt 2 …}}
```

Today: `◦ ISSUED · correlation: :checkout`; right-click the pill to find `[:checkout/failed {:status :error …}]`. Under the join: `✗ ERROR 500 · 2 attempts · 1204ms`, RESPONSE showing the elided `:error` map (`[:error :status]` per `spec/014-HTTPRequests.md:552-554`), `→ reply ↗`.

**(c) Request aborted on actor destroy.** A machine actor issued the request; the actor is destroyed while it is in flight.

```
bundle [:app/main #512]  (the destroy run)   :other [{:operation :rf.http/aborted-on-actor-destroy :tags {:request-id … :actor-id … :url …}}
                                                     {:operation :rf.http/aborted :op-type :error :tags {:reason :actor-destroyed :work/id [:rf.work/http :actor/load 1 1] …}}]
[nil :ungrouped]  {:operation :rf.http/replied :tags {:status :cancelled :rf.reply/work-id [:rf.work/http :actor/load 1 1] …}}   ; or :stale if the target was obsolete
```

Today: the issuing record reads `◦ ISSUED` for ever (and per rf2-n3sx9 the destroy bundle's own HTTP records, if any, do not take this abort). Under the join: `◌ CANCELLED :actor-destroyed`, no duration, no reply link (none was delivered).

**The shape of the framework step (option D).** One new `:info` row emitted from `managed-handler` right after the issuance number is allocated (`handlers.cljc:453-455`), inside the fx handler's scope, so it inherits the run's dispatch-id and the `reg-fx` coord for free:

```clojure
(rf.trace/emit! :info :rf.http/issued
  {:rf.reply/work-id   [:rf.work/http logical-id issuance 1]   ; (work-id normalised) — the same head the completion rows carry
   :rf.reply/work-kind :http
   :request-id         request-id                               ; nil when anonymous
   :url                (:url normalised)  :method (:method (:request normalised))
   :frame              frame-id
   :reply-to           <summary of the configured target>})     ; "target summary", per Managed-Effects §Tracing
```

plus `next-issuance!` counting anonymous requests under `(scoped-key frame-id logical-id)` exactly as it counts named ones (the same eviction on completion), so `[kind logical-id issuance]` is unique among live work for every request. The completion rows already carry that head. **No dispatch-id is captured, no invocation index is minted, no tag is added to any completion row.**
== DOSSIER (preserved verbatim, ai/decisions/rf2-6ooch.xray-http-completion-join.md, 2026-09-23) == — part 2 of 2

**A sketch of the join (option A's panel half, on that key).** In `managed_fx_helpers.cljc`, for each HTTP record in the focused bundle: read `(subvec work-id 0 3)` off the bundle's own `:rf.http/issued` row (it is in `:other`, with the record's dispatch-id — attributed by position among the bundle's `:rf.http/managed` handled rows, or simply by `:request-id` when present); then over the buffer, `filter` rows whose `:rf.reply/work-id` / `[:tags :work/id]` share that prefix, take the latest by `:time`, and read its status through `reply_envelope/work-event-row` (`reply_envelope.cljc:562-698`, already projecting every HTTP completion op to `{:phase :completed :status :ok|:error|:cancelled|:stale …}`). `duration-ms = (:time completion) − (:time issued-row)`. No completion row in the buffer → an honest `ISSUED · no completion in buffer` (which also covers ring aging; the bead's item 5). The reply-dispatch bundle is found the same way: the delivered reply map carries `:rf.reply/work-id` verbatim (`Managed-Effects.md:127-130`), so `→ reply ↗` = the `:source :http` bundle whose event's reply map has the same head.

Two further shapes the evidence rules OUT, named because a reader reaches for them:

- **A labelled best-effort join, no framework change.** Exact for the 17% with a `:request-id`, silently wrong for the 83% without (§2a). "Trust the programmer" cuts against a diagnostic that is right only when they already did the work of naming the request, and both reviewers said not to build on the heuristic. Out.
- **Stamp the issuing run's `:rf.trace/dispatch-id` onto the completion row so the grouper files it INTO the issuing bundle** (tempting, because "caller-supplied `:tags :rf.trace/dispatch-id` wins", `trace.cljc:574-575`, `009:1655`). It would make B's in-bundle collector read the completion with almost no join code — and it would be a lie about the run: 009 §Dispatch correlation defines the id as riding "every trace event emitted INSIDE that one event's pipeline run" (`009:73`), the epoch record for that run was harvested long before, and a bundle that mutates after its epoch closed breaks time-travel and the epoch-capture seam. Out.

**What the stance says.** "Excellent tools … low friction" argues for the outcome on the record — it is the first question anyone debugging an SPA asks. "Not over-engineering" argues against A's stamp (a second identity for a fact the framework already names) and for D's step 1, which is the smallest change that makes the join exact and is owed to the spec anyway. "Don't litigate the minutiae" says: do not spend a worker on the taxonomy colours or the ring-aging label before the key exists.

## 4. Recommendation

**Rule D: prioritise, in two steps, and retitle rf2-6ooch accordingly.**

Step 1 — a new S bead, framework side, dispatchable today: emit `:rf.http/issued` from `managed-handler` carrying the work-id head and the target summary (the row Managed-Effects §Tracing already requires and resources/mutations already emit), and make `next-issuance!` count anonymous issuances per (frame, logical-id) so the work-id is unique among live work for every request. Files: `implementation/http/src/re_frame/http/handlers.cljc`, `registry.cljc`, the two evict call sites in `transport.cljc`, `reply.cljc` docstrings; `spec/014-HTTPRequests.md` (one trace-event row, one sentence on anonymous issuance) and one cell of `spec/Managed-Effects.md:187`; `reply_envelope.cljc:389-398`'s table gains `:rf.http/issued :issued` (a one-line Xray edit, or leave it to the suffix heuristic — its comment says a newly-added op still classifies). Gates: `implementation/http` JVM tests (RED first: two overlapping anonymous requests from one event-id read one work-id; GREEN: two) and `npm run test:cljs` for the CLJS transport path.

**Acceptance bar for step 1:** on a JVM projection probe, each issuing bundle's `:other` holds exactly one `:rf.http/issued` row whose `[kind logical-id issuance]` equals exactly one `:rf.http/replied` row's in the buffer — for (i) a named request, (ii) a named request superseded and re-issued, (iii) two overlapping anonymous requests of one event-id, (iv) two anonymous requests in one run — with the control that before the change (iii) and (iv) share one work-id. Zero change to any delivered reply map for a named request; anonymous replies change only in the issuance digit when overlapping.

Step 2 — this bead, un-deferred once step 1 merges: the panel join on that key (§2's sketch), the closed reply taxonomy in the pill, `→ reply ↗`, `ISSUED · no completion in buffer` for the aged/pending case, fixtures derived from the producer (rf2-y8doi.28's model), tests for the four cases above plus the rf2-n3sx9 residue (explicit abort beside a same-id re-issue). Fence: rf2-y8doi.18's seven files plus `reply_envelope.cljc`. M, as the bead sizes it.

Why this over A: the bead's stamp adds a second correlation identity to rows that already carry the first; step 1 finishes the one the spec chose. Why over B: the framework half is cheap, owed, and useful on its own; deferring the whole feature leaves the ordinary request dark in the tool whose spec calls this record the hero. Why over C: nothing in the evidence says the feature is unwanted — only that it was not to be built on a heuristic, and now it need not be.

```clojure
      b (next-issuance! :frame/a :search/go)]
  ;; Anonymous B finishes first; anonymous A is still live.
  (evict-issuance-on-completion! :frame/a :search/go b)
  [a b (next-issuance! :frame/a :search/go)])
;; => [1 2 1]
```

C now shares A's work id while both are live. This exercises the **proposed extension's allocator/evictor schedule**, not a claim that the existing named supersession path leaves A running normally. Control: completing older issuance 1 while 2 remains current preserves the counter, yielding `[1 2 3]`. Separate frames each start at 1. A named request completed and subsequently reissued also yields `[1 1]`, as intended by today's eviction policy.

Consequently, matching all retained rows by `[kind logical-id issuance]` and selecting the latest gives an earlier named request a later request's outcome. Adding frame fixes cross-frame collisions, but does not fix this historical reuse. Nor is the dossier's timing premise established: the success path evicts at [transport.cljc](../../implementation/http/src/re_frame/http/transport.cljc), line 975, **before** it emits the canonical completion through lines 992 and 675–676. On the JVM, a new allocation can interleave in that interval. I verified the source order; I did not execute that concurrent interleaving. “First completion after issuance” therefore needs a proof the proposed design does not supply.

**Other findings that change the implementation brief**

A full retry history needs additional producer identity. The 5xx branch builds a raw failure without work-id at `transport.cljc:1512–1517`; `maybe-retry!` passes it into the retry handoff at line 1452; the retry emit consumes that same failure at line 2065. Its tags at lines 1107–1115 carry neither issuance nor work-id. Self-identification happens on the terminal failure path at line 876, not on this intermediate path. Thus the uncertain claim that the nested retry failure already supplies the join key is false for ordinary 5xx retries. Either stamp it explicitly or exclude detailed retry history from the first panel increment. Final attempt count can still come from a terminal reply.

Not every issuance ends in `:rf.http/replied`: supersession and obsolete actor targets have explicit non-delivery/stale paths. Conversely, an actor-destroy cancellation **can** deliver to a still-meaningful ordinary event target (`transport.cljc:789–811`). Acceptance must cover canonical terminal facts and actual observed delivery, rather than requiring one replied row for every issue or forbidding a reply link for every cancellation.

Trace timestamps already supply comparable duration endpoints (`core/trace.cljc:710–714`, `core/interop.cljs:170–189`). This agrees with the [W3C High Resolution Time clock model](https://www.w3.org/TR/hr-time-3/#sec-time-concepts): durations compare points on the same clock. Call the result **elapsed request time**; it includes retry backoff and processing and is not a measured network-only waterfall. Do not subtract epoch `:completed-at` from trace time. Missing terminal evidence should read “no completion in this capture,” without claiming the request is currently running.

**The implementation shape I recommend**

First, specify one non-recycled identity per HTTP invocation, stable across its retries, with the retry attempt remaining the final work-id component. Prefer using the existing issuance component with a constant-space allocator, such as a runtime-wide monotonic sequence, over adding a parallel attempt identity. That deliberately changes the current “first request per id/frame is 1” value contract; update the owning specification and tests explicitly. Frame-scoped cancellation and supersession must remain unchanged even if diagnostic numbering changes. Define the allocator's lifetime to cover the trace history it identifies.

This is a preference, not a requirement to implement that exact allocator. If preserving the present work-id values is the priority, explicit origin metadata identifying the issuing frame/run/invocation is a valid alternative: causal origin and retry-attempt identity answer different questions, so the one-name-per-fact rule does not automatically prohibit it. Its cost is propagation through every relevant terminal, suppression and delivery path. Retaining per-id counters plus reference counts and temporal matching looks more complicated than either option, particularly with truncated captures.

Emit a redacted `:rf.http/issued` row before transport work can synchronously finish, carrying identity, frame and target summary. Use that row itself as the anchor for an actual HTTP invocation, or prove its association with the generic handled record; same request-id alone cannot distinguish two effects in one run. Preserve generic skipped/overridden records when no real HTTP request starts. Route new URL/target data through the existing privacy machinery, rather than copying the dossier's raw illustrative tags directly. Document the trace contract in the owning specs; an existing catalogue omission is not, by itself, authority to waive documentation for a new operation.

Then build the Xray join with frame-qualified identity, canonical terminal-status precedence, observed reply-bundle links and elided response summaries. Scan/index the bounded buffer once per update and reuse that projection across focused records; avoid one full scan per record. Do not move asynchronous completions into the issuing epoch by rewriting their dispatch-id. This increment delivers the valuable outcome and navigation; it does not by itself complete 019's app-db-diff story.

Before the panel depends on the producer, require transport-derived fixtures for anonymous siblings in one run, reverse-order anonymous completion with a third issuance, sequential reuse after completion, named supersession, sibling frames, explicit abort beside same-id issue, retry then success, and suppressed versus delivered actor cancellation. Verify incomplete captures stay unattributed, and allocation state stays bounded. These are direct counterexamples and lifecycle boundaries, not a request for a broad redesign.

**Limits:** I executed the isolated allocator probe, not the JVM/CLJS transport suites, a browser session or a performance benchmark. I inspected existing integration tests but did not rerun them. I did not independently reproduce the dossier's teaching-corpus census, and example frequency would not establish runtime collision frequency anyway. The user benefit supports prioritisation; the evidence does not support the dossier's S estimate or its claim that unchanged eviction makes the join exact. The next authorised implementation task should settle that identity contract and prove it, with the panel depending on that result.

> Posture is that we are pre-alpha and focused on elegance, power and a masterpiece.

> last fine detail and drown in the minutiae.

## What this feature is

The 019 F.1 / F-C2 "wire-boundary" hero record for `:rf.http/managed`: the Epoch panel's managed-fx record shows the real outcome of the request — `OK 200 · 82ms`, `ERROR :rf.http/transport`, `CANCELLED :actor-destroyed`, `IN-FLIGHT` — by joining the runtime's completion rows to the issuing `:rf.fx/handled` across the WHOLE trace buffer. After rf2-y8doi.18 (B) lands, the HTTP record honestly says only `ISSUED`; this feature is what would make it say more.

## Why it cannot land in the issuing bundle (the fact B rests on; verify at your trunk with a control)

`emit!` and `emit-error!` take the dispatch-id from the dynamic `*handler-scope*` (`implementation/core/src/re_frame/trace.cljc` ~:863-865, ~:906-907). Every HTTP row after issuance is emitted from the transport callback with no scope (`:rf.http/replied` at `implementation/http/src/re_frame/http/transport.cljc` ~:557, "OUTSIDE any with-frame scope" ~:538-541; the failure kinds at ~:919 via `(rf.trace/emit-error! (:kind failure) redacted)`; `:rf.http/retry-attempt` ~:1107) or inside a DIFFERENT run's drain (`:rf.http/aborted-on-actor-destroy` at `implementation/http/src/re_frame/http/registry.cljc` ~:869 inside the destroying run; `:rf.http/stale-suppressed` ~:622/~:705/registry ~:927 inside the superseding run). The grouper files scope-less rows under `[nil :ungrouped]` (`implementation/core/src/re_frame/trace/projection.cljc` ~:142-159, ~:189-199). The ONE exception: a synchronous body-prep failure (`transport.cljc` ~:2072-2086) emits the failure row inside the fx handler's own stack, i.e. inside the issuing drain — B's record already handles that case.

## The A design (from the rf2-y8doi.18 dossier)

- `tools/xray/src/day8/re_frame2_xray/panels/managed_fx_subs.cljs` adds `[:rf.xray/trace-buffer]` as a composite input (the resources composite already does exactly this: `tools/xray/src/day8/re_frame2_xray/panels/resources.cljs` ~:1391-1394).
- `tools/xray/src/day8/re_frame2_xray/panels/managed_fx_helpers.cljc` gains a join: for each issuing `:rf.fx/handled`, find the `:rf.http/replied` / failure-kind / `retry-attempt` / `aborted-on-actor-destroy` / `stale-suppressed` rows for that request anywhere in the buffer and read `:status` off the completion row. The reader already exists: `tools/xray/src/day8/re_frame2_xray/panels/reply_envelope.cljc` `work-event-row` (~:562-698) projects every family's completion row to `{:phase :completed :status :ok|:error|:cancelled|:stale :work-id … :completed-at …}` and already names `:rf.http/replied` (~:416).
- Taxonomy: the panel's `:ok | :error | :in-flight | :overridden | :skipped | :stub` (+ `:issued` after B) is replaced for HTTP by the framework's closed reply statuses (`spec/Managed-Effects.md` ~:160-168 per the dossier — verify) plus one non-reply status for "no completion row in the buffer yet"; `common-record` (~:452-484) stops folding a cancel into `:error`; `status-pill` gains two colours/glyphs; `:http-status` reads `[:meta :status]` on ok and `[:error :status]` on 4xx/5xx (`spec/014-HTTPRequests.md` ~:552-554).
- RESPONSE section ceiling: `trace-summary` routes `:value` and `:meta` through the elision walker (`implementation/core/src/re_frame/reply.cljc` ~:618-626), so on-box it is a summary and under `:sensitive?` it is the `:rf/redacted` sentinel. 019 F.1's "Response: 200 OK { :order-id … }" is the ceiling, not the floor.

## Why it is HEURISTIC today (both reviewers; do not build on this without fixing it)

1. The join key. The completion row carries `:rf.reply/work-id [:rf.work/http logical-id issuance attempt]` (`implementation/http/src/re_frame/http/reply.cljc` ~:84-98), where `logical-id` is the caller's `:request-id` when supplied else the originating event-id, and `issuance` / `attempt` are counters the issuing `:rf.fx/handled` does NOT carry. So the join is logical-id plus "first completion row after the issue time" — exact for the common case, ambiguous under precisely the storm cases the persona hunts: the same `:request-id` re-issued (supersession: the superseded attempt's `stale-suppressed` and the superseder's `replied` share a logical-id) and concurrent same-event requests with no `:request-id`. Codex: "the proposed request-id/time heuristic cannot reliably attribute overlapping requests."
2. The clocks. Trace `:time` uses `now-ms` (`implementation/core/src/re_frame/trace.cljc` ~:713), which on CLJS is `performance.now()` (origin-relative); the completion row's `:completed-at` is `epoch-now-ms` (`implementation/core/src/re_frame/interop.cljs` ~:170-189; `transport.cljc` ~:354-377 `reply-ctx`). Subtracting them yields a meaningless duration in the SPA. A's `:duration-ms` needs one clock: either the completion row's own `:time` (trace clock) minus the issue row's `:time`, or a framework-stamped issue epoch.
3. Exact linkage wants a FRAMEWORK change, not a panel change. The dossier proposed a `:rf.reply/origin-dispatch-id` tag on `:rf.http/replied`; Codex showed a dispatch-id alone cannot distinguish two HTTP effects issued by one event — the stamp must identify the invocation (per-effect index within the issuing run) AND the frame. That is a `spec/014-HTTPRequests.md` + `spec/009-Instrumentation.md` catalogue change (009 is HOT-ZONE) and lands in `implementation/http/src/re_frame/http/transport.cljc` / `reply.cljc` before the panel join can be exact.
4. A completion join alone still does not implement F.1's handler-and-app-db story (`tools/xray/spec/019-Cross-Cutting-Insight.md` ~:546-590): "handler dispatched" and "Applied:" need the reply-dispatch bundle and ITS app-db diff, keyed the same exact way.
5. Ring-buffer aging can split an issue row and its reply across the ring boundary (the rf2-y8doi.12 reviewer's mutation note), so "no completion yet" and "completion aged out" are indistinguishable without a ledger read.
6. Performance: the composite recomputes per trace tick rather than per focus move (the rf2-y8doi.12 #7 class); bounded only if the join pre-filters to `:rf.http/*` rows.
7. The "exchange is one right-click away" escape route B leaned on is itself broken: the `:http-correlation` typed filter matches a flat `:correlation-id` tag no producer stamps. That is its own bug bead (discovered-from rf2-y8doi.18, filed the same day); fix it first, since its "what is an exchange" design is the same question this join answers.

## If Mike picks this up — order of work

1. Framework stamp first (separate bead; touches spec/014, spec/009 [HOT-ZONE], the transport and reply namespaces, http tests): the completion row names the issuing run exactly (dispatch-id + frame + invocation index) and both endpoints carry one comparable clock.
2. Then the panel join on the exact key (this bead): helpers (join + taxonomy), subs (input), template (two pills), producer-derived fixtures (C16's model, rf2-y8doi.28), tests for supersession and no-`:request-id` cases. ## Problem

`rf/feature-loaded?` (`core.cljc:2860` → `features.cljc:113`) and `rf/require-feature!` (`core.cljc:2869` → `features.cljc:160`) have zero non-test code consumers after 34 example boots, four tools, two scaffolds and a Ring host — only skill prose (`skills/re-frame2/patterns/resources.md:17`, `resources-mutations.md:7`) and the cheatsheet (`:191-192`). `feature-loaded?` is `(some? (late-bind/get-fn probe-key))` ≡ `(get-in (rf/features) [k :loaded?])`; `require-feature!` throws the same Maven coordinate every late-bound facade fn already throws on first call (`late_bind.cljc:228`, `API.md:891`). `features` is the one inventory and STAYS (data before magic).

## Target

```clojure
(rf/features)                              ; → {:epoch {:maven … :require … :spec … :loaded? true} …} — shape unchanged
(get-in (rf/features) [:epoch :loaded?])   ; the boolean. An UNKNOWN key reads nil here where feature-loaded? read
                                           ; false — teach the lookup; do not claim identical return contracts.

;; The early production guard, for an app that wants boot-time failure rather than first-call failure.
;; One line, no framework verb, NOT an assert (asserts are elidable):
(when-not (get-in (rf/features) [:epoch :loaded?])
  (throw (ex-info "re-frame.epoch is not on the classpath" (get (rf/features) :epoch))))
```

Codex's caution is honoured, not waved away: `require-feature!` gave an EARLY, structured preflight error that first-operation failure does not replace. description:

## Problem

Two shipped public vars had the whole tool corpus (Xray, Story, two MCP servers, the pair preload) as their audience for months and drew zero calls.

**`group-by-event-with-events`** — `implementation/core/src/re_frame/trace/projection.cljc:337-363`, facade re-export `core.cljc:2321-2337` (with a facade-classification comment naming "re-frame2-pair streaming event bundles" as its consumer). Consumers outside `implementation/**/test`: **0** — `git grep -l -F 'group-by-event-with-events' -- ':!ai/'` → 8 files: the two defs, `docs/api/re-frame.core.md`, `spec/API.md`, the two manifest EDNs, `elision_test.clj` (a comment at `:538`), `trace/projection_cljs_test.cljc` (three deftests, `:127-190`). Its stated consumer reads bundles from the ring (`runtime.cljs:1467-1482`), and the ring's bundles already carry `:trace-events` per run (`tooling.cljc:506-518`) — `(trace-buffer f)` returns this exact shape by default. The manifest row itself records the doubt: `api-manifest.edn:125` "RECORDED UNCERTAINTY (existence, not placement): … zero non-test in-repo consumers … whether it should exist at all".

**`projected-history`** — `implementation/epoch/src/re_frame/epoch.cljc:733-739` → `epoch/tool_pair.cljc:2074-2081` (body: `(mapv #(projected-record % opts) (state/history-for frame-id))`), facade `core.cljc:2493-2512` via `core_epoch.cljc:258-272` (`defwrapper`, `:on-absent :empty-vec`) and the hook `:epoch/projected-history` (`late_bind/directory.cljc:879-882`). Code consumers outside framework tests: **0** — under `tools/` the only hit is a docstring (`re-frame2-pair-mcp/.../tools/epoch_egress.cljs:18`). The one real off-box consumer, pair-mcp `epoch_egress.cljs:193,245`, emits `(re-frame.core/projected-record r# opts)` per record over a **paged** subset — it pages first, then projects, which is the composition `projected-history` cannot express and which its own docstring forbids ("MUST call `projected-history` rather than walking … the hand-walk is one missed `mapv projected-record` away from leaking", `core.cljc:2497-2504`, "kept per rf2-p7vf9"). The docstring guards nobody; the one consumer that exists is the "anti-pattern", correctly.

## Target API

None added. Composition replaces both:

```clojure
;; fold + keep raw events — the ring already does it
(rf/trace-buffer frame-id)                                   ; bundles carry :trace-events
;; whole-ring off-box egress — select, then project each record
(mapv #(rf/projected-record % opts) (rf/epoch-history frame-id))
```

`group-by-event` (`projection.cljc:291`) and `domino-bucket` (`:78`) are untouched (Xray `self_noise.cljc:152` + 15 tool prose refs use the projection ns). `projected-record` is untouched — it is `@egress.n`'s.

## Corroboration

One-reviewer area; codex concurs on both with one stated limitation each. On `group-by-event-with-events`: "Retiring the unused richer projection is reasonable demand pruning, but state that limitation" — it transforms an arbitrary supplied stream while `trace-buffer` reads a live ring, so they are not substitutes for imported / filtered / cross-frame streams (no such consumer exists; if one appears, `group-by-event` plus a `group-by` on the same `bundle-key` is the composition — record this in the PR body and wherever 009 §Event-bundle projection mentions the `-with-events` variant). On `projected-history`: "a better removal candidate: the real off-box consumer pages first and already applies `projected-record` to the chosen values. Preserve that projection-before-egress requirement." `@egress.n`'s full target deletes `projected-record` and `projected-history` together; this bead is a subset of it and is compatible with either outcome of that ruling — if @egress.n is ruled and dispatched first, drop this bead's `projected-history` half.

`group-by-event-with-events`: `core.cljc:2321-2337` (comment + def); `projection.cljc:337-363`; `spec/api-manifest.edn:125`; `spec/api-manifest-metadata.edn:1427`; `spec/API.md:625` (row; **hot-zone**); `docs/api/re-frame.core.md:1042-1049`; `projection_cljs_test.cljc:127-190` (three deftests — but keep the FACT `group-by-event-with-events-isolates-trace-events-by-frame` pins, re-homed: assert on `(trace-buffer f)` bundles that `:trace-events` holds only that frame's events; `trace_buffer_test.clj` may already pin it — check before adding); `elision_test.clj:538` comment.

`projected-history`: `epoch.cljc:733-739`; `tool_pair.cljc:2074-2081` and its docstring mentions `:4`, `:24`; `core_epoch.cljc:258-272`; `core.cljc:2493-2512`; `directory.cljc:879-882` (the `:epoch/projected-history` entry — the directory is a closed roster, so the key leaves with it); `epoch/state.cljc:874` comment; `spec/api-manifest.edn:140` (core) and `:196` (epoch); `api-manifest-metadata.edn:1498`, `:2045`; `docs/api/re-frame.core.md:4` (intro list) and `:1255-1263`; `docs/api/re-frame.epoch.md:210-222`; `spec/API.md:26` (the re-export list) and `:43` (**hot-zone**); `spec/Tool-Pair.md:88` ("(and `projected-history`)"; **hot-zone**); `spec/009-Instrumentation.md:2273` (mention in the `:rf.error/epoch-artefact-missing` row; **hot-zone**); `spec/Privacy.md:123` (row → rewrite as the composition, keeping the normative sentence "every record that crosses a process boundary passes through `projected-record`"), `:116`, `:321`, `:550`; `migration/from-re-frame-v1/observability-logging-sweep.md:387`; pair-mcp `epoch_egress.cljs:18` docstring (name `projected-record` as the single normative emission site — it already is at `:193,:245`).

title: Test-suite pruning, fifth pass: tools/story play/, recorder/ and theme/
description:
Child of rf2-nvxtm (test-suite pruning, fifth pass). One worktree, one PR.

SURFACE: tools/story play/, recorder/ and theme/. This is the surface of rf2-txsk5.8 (fourth pass). Read rf2-txsk5.8 first: its description, notes and close reason. Together they give the runners and lanes, the count floors, the surface's cautions, the covers it relied on, and what the fourth pass already pruned. rf2-txsk5.8 gives the exact files in scope, or names the third-pass bead (rf2-n6gq4.8) that does. Confirm the scope and the runners yourself at tip in step 1, and report the delta.

<DIR> in the prompt below means this surface.

REPO MECHANICS: read rf2-nvxtm's description. Its count-floor, CLJS-lane, test-name, cross-surface-cover, hot-zone, plant and one-PR rules apply in full, and they win over anything in the prompt that seems to conflict.

== THE PROMPT (verbatim from Mike's local prompt file, which is not checked in; also in rf2-nvxtm's description)

Simplify the unit tests under tools/story play/, recorder/ and theme/. Do not change the code under test. LLMs tend to
write too many low-value unit tests, and this suite was largely written by them.

Assume the suite has more tests than it needs, and that many of its tests are longer
than they need to be. Every test costs CI time, reading time and refactoring friction,
and the low-value ones hide the tests that matter. I want a lean suite: each test earns
its place by guarding a behaviour a caller relies on, against a regression that could
plausibly happen and would matter. Each surviving test should be as short as the thing
it proves.

Stay inside tools/story play/, recorder/ and theme/. Do not edit tests elsewhere. If a deletion relies on a test outside
tools/story play/, recorder/ and theme/ to keep covering something, name that test in your report.

Work in this order:
1. Run the suite and record the result: tests, assertions, failures, lines. Confirm a
   runner actually executes each file in tools/story play/, recorder/ and theme/; a file nothing runs cannot be pruned on
   evidence, so report it.
2. Read the code under test and list what it promises its callers: normal results, each
   boundary that takes its own path, each promised failure, and any past bug the tests
   refer to.
3. Map every test to the promise it checks. Most of the work shows up in this map:
   promises with five tests, tests with no promise, and tests of something no caller
   relies on.
4. Decide each test: keep, simplify, merge or delete.
5. Run the suite again and prove the pruned suite still guards every promise.

Work in small batches by contract group, and commit as you go. Before each batch,
predict the change in test and assertion counts; after it, confirm the counts moved by
exactly that much. If helper agents are available, use read-only ones for the mapping
step. If tools/story play/, recorder/ and theme/ plainly will not finish in about four hours, stop at a group boundary,
ship what is done, and list the files you did not reach.

Decide each test with two questions:
- If this test were deleted, what bug could ship that no remaining test would catch?
  If you cannot name one, delete it.
- If you can name one: is that bug plausible in this code, would a caller notice it,
  and would nothing else surface it at once (a compile or load error, a boot-time
  validation, most of the suite going red)? If the bug is implausible, harmless, or
  loud anyway, delete the test.

Delete:
- A test another test implies. If A cannot pass while B fails, drop B.
- Extra examples of one behaviour that take the same path through the code.
- Existence and smoke checks: a function exists, a var resolves, something "is
  registered", a result is non-nil, a call "does not throw", when another test
  exercises the same call with a real assertion.
- Change detectors: a test that copies a constant, a data table, a default config, a
  roster or a string out of the source and asserts equality. It fails on every intended
  change and catches no bug. The exception is a value callers depend on exactly, such as
  a public id or a documented default, that nothing else pins: keep one test for it.
- Absence checks for things nothing produces, and negative-input tests for inputs no
  caller passes and the contract does not mention.
- Exhaustive enumeration: one row per enum member, keyword or field when they all take
  one path. Keep one representative plus the members that take a different path.
- Tests of the language, a library or the framework: a constructor sets a field, a
  getter returns it, a map holds the key just put in it.
- Tests that pin how the code works instead of what it does: private helpers already
  exercised through the public path, call order, internal data shapes, greps of the
  implementation's own source, and log, trace or error wording that is not part of the
  contract.
- Tests whose expected value is computed by the same logic as the code under test.
- Assertions that a mock returned what it was told to return, and tests whose mock setup
  is most of the test while the assertion checks the mock.
- Separate per-platform test files asserting the same thing about platform-neutral code.
  A single shared test that runs on both platforms is one test, not two: keep it.
- Tests of test helpers and fixtures.
- Tests of code that has no logic in it, and tests whose only subject is production code
  that no production caller uses.

Simplify every test you keep:
- Assert the whole result with one equality instead of one assertion per field. Drop an
  assertion that a later one in the same test implies.
- Cut setup, fixtures and data to what the assertion needs. Remove unused bindings,
  requires, helpers and fixtures.
- Tests that vary one input become one table-driven test. Keep the boundary rows and
  drop the mid-range ones.
- Tests that repeat the same setup for one assertion each become one test.
- Delete comments and docstrings that restate the code or narrate history. Keep a
  one-line why where a test's purpose is not obvious from its name and body.
- Rename a test only when its name no longer says what it asserts, and first check that
  nothing matches on the name, such as a CI filter, a skip list or a doc that cites it.

Keep, however small:
- The only test of a promise a caller relies on: a normal result, a boundary that takes
  a different path (empty, one, many; zero; the limit and one past it), a promised
  failure.
- A regression test for a bug that actually happened, unless a stronger test now covers
  it.
- The last guard of a security, privacy or redaction promise.
- The last test that keeps a gate able to fail, and the last test holding a published
  doc or spec claim to the code.
When a weak test and a strong test overlap, keep the strong one: the one that would fail
on more bugs.

Do not:
- Weaken an assertion, or swap an exact check for a looser one, to make a merge or a
  simplification easier.
- Delete a test because it fails, is slow or is flaky. Report it.
- Leave unused helpers, fixtures or requires behind.
- Add new tests. If you find a promise with no test, report it.
- Change production code. Dead code and stale docs or spec text go in your report as a
  list, not into your change.
If anything pins test counts or names, such as a count floor or a roster, update it in
the same change. Commit one file or module at a time.

Prove it:
- The suite passes before and after. Report both sets of counts.
- For each group of deletions that rests on a surviving cover, break the code in a place
  the deleted tests guarded and confirm a surviving test fails. Then restore the code and
  confirm it matches the committed file. One plant per group sharing a cover is enough.
  If nothing fails, you removed real coverage: put the tests back.
- A cover must actually run. A skipped test, a fixture the runner never loads, or a test
  on a lane nothing executes covers nothing. Confirm the runner executes a cover before
  resting a deletion on it.
- Run each test file you touched on its own at least once. Deleting a file can break a
  sibling that relied on it loading something first; give such a file its own require.
- A deletion made under the second question needs no plant. Give its one-line reason in
  the report instead.
- A simplification must not change what a test can catch. Where you removed an
  assertion, name the assertion that implies it.

Report:
- Before and after: tests, assertions, lines.
- Deleted tests, grouped by reason. For each, the surviving cover, or the one-line
  reason it was not worth keeping.
- Merges and simplifications: what went into what, and the lines each file lost.
- Notable keeps: tests you considered deleting but kept, and why.
- Plants, and which test caught each.
- Tests outside tools/story play/, recorder/ and theme/ that your deletions rely on.
- Dead code, stale docs or spec text, and gaps (promises with no test). One line each.

If you are unsure whether a promise a caller relies on is still covered, keep the test
and say so. Losing the only guard of a real promise is still the one mistake that matters
more than leaving an extra test in. But being unsure whether a test is worth keeping is
not a reason to keep it. If you cannot say in one line what plausible regression it
catches that a caller would notice, delete it.

title: Registered views warn on valid composition: delete the non-DOM-root console warning and its warn-once cache
description:
Registered views warn about valid composition. Delete the non-DOM-root console warning and its warn-once cache.

## What happens today

A `reg-view` whose root is another component, a fragment, an interop head or a Form-3 class gets a one-shot `console.warn`: `[re-frame] reg-view <id> — root element is …; data-rf2-source-coord skipped`.
- `implementation/core/src/re_frame/views/source_coord_annotation.cljs` (~L160 and ~L200) calls `rf.views.warn-once/warn-non-dom-root!`.
- `implementation/core/src/re_frame/substrate/spine.cljs` `make-warn-non-dom-root-fn` does the same for the React-hook adapters.
- The text comes from `non-dom-root-warning` in `implementation/core/src/re_frame/adapter/context.cljs`.

## Why it should go

Every one of those roots is valid composition. The only "repair" is a wrapper element, and Spec 006's mutate-not-wrap rule forbids exactly that. The Reagent adapter's own recipe trips the warning: `implementation/adapters/reagent/README.md` (~L108) shows an outer view returning `[(rf/view :my-app.charts/vega-inner) spec]`, and the inner view returns a `create-class`.

Nothing depends on the warning:
- Pair tools already fall back to `(rf/handler-meta {:source :store :kind :view :id id})` for an unannotated root.
- `test-quiet` buffers `console.warn` so that green runs stay quiet.
- Fresco already declined this clause for the same reason (spec/006 "One clause is deliberately NOT taken").

This is the project stance at work: trust the programmer, and warn on failures, not on legal code.

## Change

Delete:
- the warning and its warn-once cache (`warned-non-dom-roots`, `warn-non-dom-root!`, `non-dom-root-warning`, `make-warn-non-dom-root-fn`);
- their governance enrolments;
- the `^:no-doc` re-export `re-frame.views/clear-warned-non-dom-roots!` (no manifest row);
- the tests that assert the warning.

Preserve:
- DOM-root annotation (both attributes);
- silent pass-through of exempt roots (Form-3 class identity, interop heads);
- the registry fallback;
- the `:adapter/clear-warn-once-caches!` chain, which still clears `:views/seen-render-keys`.

Add no option and no replacement diagnostic.

This reverses Spec 006's MUST at ~L489 (also ~L505, ~L556, ~L568) and the "KEEP" in reagent-slim `IMPL-SPEC.md` §14.6. That KEEP recorded shipped reality and was not a ruling. Also update `tools/xray/spec/Conventions.md` (~L189-193) and `IMPL-SPEC.md` §11.3.

## Files

- Core: `implementation/core/src/re_frame/views/{warn_once,source_coord_annotation}.cljs`, `views.cljs`, `adapter/context.cljs`, `substrate/spine.cljs`, and the comments in `late_bind.cljc` / `test_support.cljc`.
- Test-quiet: the `implementation/test-quiet/src/re_frame/test_quiet/shadow_node.cljs` docstring.
- Tests: `adapters/reagent/test/**/source_coord_warn_once_cljs_test.cljs`, `warn_once_fixture_isolation_cljs_test.cljs`, `core/test/**/views/source_coord_warn_parity_cljs_test.cljs`, `warn_once_clear_governance*`, `adapter/react_shared_suite.cljs`, `elision_probe.cljs`, and the uix / slim-form3 / fresco shared-suite entries.
- Spec: **spec/006-ReactiveSubstrate.md is a HOT-ZONE file.**

## Sequencing

This depends on the Form-2 render-evidence bead, which edits `source_coord_annotation.cljs` first.

Four reports propose this deletion: Opus core-public-api action 7, core-observability action 8, adapters action 9 and core-reactive-substrate action 3, plus Sol 09 §3 and Sol 17 §4. Supporting detail, local to this machine only: `C:\Users\miket\code\re-frame2\ai\findings\advisarial-review\opus-history\2026-10-15-low-hanging-fruit\before\adapters.md` §12, and `C:\Users\miket\code\re-frame2\ai\findings\advisarial-review\sol-history\2026-10-15-low-hanging-fruit\before\17-adapter-reagent.md` §4.

4. The warn-once governance test still passes, with `:views/seen-render-keys` still enrolled.

title: The quiet test runners ignore RF2_VERBOSE_TESTS and drop buffered stderr when a namespace or :once fixture throws
description:
The quiet test runners ignore `RF2_VERBOSE_TESTS`, and they drop buffered stderr when a run throws. Both gaps cost AI pairs real time.

## 1. A green run names no namespace

`:begin-test-ns` in `implementation/test-quiet/src/re_frame/test_quiet.cljc` only pushes onto a stack, so a green JVM or CLJS-node run never says which namespaces ran. CLAUDE.md instrument hazard (z) exists because of this. `RF2_VERBOSE_TESTS=1` is the repo's opt-in for green-path detail (`docs/quiet-tests.md`; `lib/browser-test-report.cjs` `isVerboseTests`), but neither quiet runner reads it. The runner's only `getenv` is the min-tests floor (`test_quiet/runner.clj` ~L617).

Change: under the flag, `:begin-test-ns` calls the existing `print-namespace-banner!`.
- On the JVM, read the flag via `System/getenv`.
- On CLJS, guard it with `(exists? js/process)`.

Each namespace reached then prints `Testing <ns>` once; a failure must not print it again. Default output must not change.

## 2. A throw loses the evidence

`re-frame.test-quiet.runner/-main` replays the stderr ring only from its `:summary` hook. Two failures propagate out of `(apply cognitect.test-runner/-main …)`, which has no catch around it, so the warnings just before the throw are lost:
- a namespace that throws on require;
- a throwing `:once` fixture.

The existing `namespace-load-throw-exits-nonzero` test checks only the exit code and a marker.

Change: catch Throwable around that call, replay the ring to `original-err` under a header, and rethrow.

## Do not

- Rebuild the runner around cognitect's `test`.
- Touch the banner filter. That is a separate open question.
- Edit CLAUDE.md.

No hot-zone file.

Supporting detail, local to this machine only: `C:\Users\miket\code\re-frame2\ai\findings\advisarial-review\sol-history\2026-10-15-low-hanging-fruit\before\33-test-quiet.md` §1 and §3.

description:

title: Epoch replay finds its own epoch through a four-times-patched commit-observation protocol; select by the router's minted dispatch-id and delete it
description:
Replay finds its own epoch through a one-shot commit-observation protocol that has been patched four times. The router already mints a dispatch-id for every dispatch, so select by that and delete the protocol.

## Where

`perform-replay!` in `implementation/epoch/src/re_frame/epoch/tool_pair.cljc` (~L773, `(let [observation (rf.epoch.state/arm-commit-observation! frame-id)`) rediscovers its own dispatch through a one-shot observation. The machinery is:
- `arm-commit-observation!`;
- `note-observed-dispatch!`, fed from `capture.cljc` (~L235);
- `note-commit!` and `take-observed-commit!`;
- an ~80-line rationale in `epoch/state.cljc` (~L275-450).

Each of its rules was added by a fix: rf2-fzbj.19, rf2-k0nr, rf2-c74lr, rf2-1mudg.

The identity already exists:
- the router mints it at `implementation/core/src/re_frame/router.cljc` (~L236): `(when rf.interop/debug-enabled? (next-dispatch-id))`;
- every epoch record carries it (`epoch/assembly.cljc` ~L366).

## Change

Add an internal router entry that runs `dispatch-sync!` and returns the minted id. Replay then selects the retained record whose `:dispatch-id` matches.

Keep public `dispatch-sync`'s return value unchanged. `core.cljc` (~L212) aliases `rf.router/dispatch-sync!` directly, so the id must not leak through it.

Preserve:
- nil when the record was evicted or never committed (never a newer child's record);
- the incarnation fence;
- the strict-input refusals.

Re-seam the JVM cross-thread test that redefines `arm-commit-observation!` (`epoch_replay_cljs_test.cljc` ~L429); do not drop it.

title: A custom SSR error projector returning nil gets the locked 500, so every app re-types the default's 404/400 rules; fall through to the default
description:
When a custom SSR error projector returns `nil`, the request gets the locked generic 500, so every custom projector has to re-implement the default's rules. Make `nil` fall through to the default projector.

## Where

`project-error` in `implementation/ssr/src/re_frame/ssr/error_projector.cljc` (~L312) treats any non-conforming result, `nil` included, as a projector failure: the locked generic 500, plus an always-on `:rf.error/sanitised-on-projection`.

So a custom projector must re-type every rule of `default-error-projector-fn`, or those cases silently become 500s:
- the route-miss 404, gated on `:kind :route`;
- the `:rf.error/no-such-route` 404;
- the `:rf.error/cofx-value-invalid` 400;
- the 400 gated on `:where :event`.

`reg-error-projector`'s own docstring example re-types two of these.

## Change

When the configured projector returns `nil`, apply `default-error-projector-fn` to the same trace event, with no record.

Preserve:
- a throw, or a non-nil wrong shape, still gives the locked 500 with the sanitised record;
- `non-projection-eligible-errors`;
- highest-status settlement;
- `:dev-error-detail?`.

Shorten the docstring example to one app case that returns nil otherwise.

Update:
- `spec/011-SSR.md` §Server error projection (~L1219). It is the one `i/crlf` file in the repo: edit it with the Edit/Write tools and check CR == CRLF afterwards.
- `docs/api/re-frame.ssr.md` and any custom-projector sample under `docs/ssr/`.
- The `spec/API.md` prose "the projector-fn signature is `(fn [trace-event] :rf/public-error)`" (~L363). This is prose only: no public name moves, and the manifests stay unchanged.

## Sequencing

**`spec/API.md` is a HOT ZONE**; the tombstone-deletion bead edits it after this one. `spec/011-SSR.md` is also edited by rf2-e2x5y and rf2-we5zf, so sequence with them.

description:
Apply the exact requested pruning prompt recursively to tools/story-mcp/test. This is a distinct worker cluster under rf2-0wcq5. Production code remains unchanged except temporary hash-verified fault plants. Push a draft test-only PR, babysit all latest-head checks to green, then mark ready. A measured no-op or unexecuted-file report is valid; do not manufacture changes.

Simplify the unit tests under tools/story-mcp/test. Do not change the code under test. LLMs tend to
write too many low-value unit tests, and this suite was largely written by them.

Assume the suite has more tests than it needs, and that many of its tests are longer
than they need to be. Every test costs CI time, reading time and refactoring friction,
and the low-value ones hide the tests that matter. I want a lean suite: each test earns
its place by guarding a behaviour a caller relies on, against a regression that could
plausibly happen and would matter. Each surviving test should be as short as the thing
it proves.

Stay inside tools/story-mcp/test. Do not edit tests elsewhere. If a deletion relies on a test outside
tools/story-mcp/test to keep covering something, name that test in your report.

Work in this order:
1. Run the suite and record the result: tests, assertions, failures, lines. Confirm a
   runner actually executes each file in tools/story-mcp/test; a file nothing runs cannot be pruned on
   evidence, so report it.
2. Read the code under test and list what it promises its callers: normal results, each
   boundary that takes its own path, each promised failure, and any past bug the tests
   refer to.
3. Map every test to the promise it checks. Most of the work shows up in this map:
   promises with five tests, tests with no promise, and tests of something no caller
   relies on.
4. Decide each test: keep, simplify, merge or delete.
5. Run the suite again and prove the pruned suite still guards every promise.

Work in small batches by contract group, and commit as you go. Before each batch,
predict the change in test and assertion counts; after it, confirm the counts moved by
exactly that much. If helper agents are available, use read-only ones for the mapping
step. If tools/story-mcp/test plainly will not finish in about four hours, stop at a group boundary,
ship what is done, and list the files you did not reach.

Decide each test with two questions:
- If this test were deleted, what bug could ship that no remaining test would catch?
  If you cannot name one, delete it.
- If you can name one: is that bug plausible in this code, would a caller notice it,
  and would nothing else surface it at once (a compile or load error, a boot-time
  validation, most of the suite going red)? If the bug is implausible, harmless, or
  loud anyway, delete the test.

Delete:
- A test another test implies. If A cannot pass while B fails, drop B.
- Extra examples of one behaviour that take the same path through the code.
- Existence and smoke checks: a function exists, a var resolves, something "is
  registered", a result is non-nil, a call "does not throw", when another test
  exercises the same call with a real assertion.
- Change detectors: a test that copies a constant, a data table, a default config, a
  roster or a string out of the source and asserts equality. It fails on every intended
  change and catches no bug. The exception is a value callers depend on exactly, such as
  a public id or a documented default, that nothing else pins: keep one test for it.
- Absence checks for things nothing produces, and negative-input tests for inputs no
  caller passes and the contract does not mention.
- Exhaustive enumeration: one row per enum member, keyword or field when they all take
  one path. Keep one representative plus the members that take a different path.
- Tests of the language, a library or the framework: a constructor sets a field, a
  getter returns it, a map holds the key just put in it.
- Tests that pin how the code works instead of what it does: private helpers already
  exercised through the public path, call order, internal data shapes, greps of the
  implementation's own source, and log, trace or error wording that is not part of the
  contract.
- Tests whose expected value is computed by the same logic as the code under test.
- Assertions that a mock returned what it was told to return, and tests whose mock setup
  is most of the test while the assertion checks the mock.
- Separate per-platform test files asserting the same thing about platform-neutral code.
  A single shared test that runs on both platforms is one test, not two: keep it.
- Tests of test helpers and fixtures.
- Tests of code that has no logic in it, and tests whose only subject is production code
  that no production caller uses.

Simplify every test you keep:
- Assert the whole result with one equality instead of one assertion per field. Drop an
  assertion that a later one in the same test implies.
- Cut setup, fixtures and data to what the assertion needs. Remove unused bindings,
  requires, helpers and fixtures.
- Tests that vary one input become one table-driven test. Keep the boundary rows and
  drop the mid-range ones.
- Tests that repeat the same setup for one assertion each become one test.
- Delete comments and docstrings that restate the code or narrate history. Keep a
  one-line why where a test's purpose is not obvious from its name and body.
- Rename a test only when its name no longer says what it asserts, and first check that
  nothing matches on the name, such as a CI filter, a skip list or a doc that cites it.

Keep, however small:
- The only test of a promise a caller relies on: a normal result, a boundary that takes
  a different path (empty, one, many; zero; the limit and one past it), a promised
  failure.
- A regression test for a bug that actually happened, unless a stronger test now covers
  it.
- The last guard of a security, privacy or redaction promise.
- The last test that keeps a gate able to fail, and the last test holding a published
  doc or spec claim to the code.
When a weak test and a strong test overlap, keep the strong one: the one that would fail
on more bugs.

Do not:
- Weaken an assertion, or swap an exact check for a looser one, to make a merge or a
  simplification easier.
- Delete a test because it fails, is slow or is flaky. Report it.
- Leave unused helpers, fixtures or requires behind.
- Add new tests. If you find a promise with no test, report it.
- Change production code. Dead code and stale docs or spec text go in your report as a
  list, not into your change.
If anything pins test counts or names, such as a count floor or a roster, update it in
the same change. Commit one file or module at a time.

Prove it:
- The suite passes before and after. Report both sets of counts.
- For each group of deletions that rests on a surviving cover, break the code in a place
  the deleted tests guarded and confirm a surviving test fails. Then restore the code and
  confirm it matches the committed file. One plant per group sharing a cover is enough.
  If nothing fails, you removed real coverage: put the tests back.
- A cover must actually run. A skipped test, a fixture the runner never loads, or a test
  on a lane nothing executes covers nothing. Confirm the runner executes a cover before
  resting a deletion on it.
- Run each test file you touched on its own at least once. Deleting a file can break a
  sibling that relied on it loading something first; give such a file its own require.
- A deletion made under the second question needs no plant. Give its one-line reason in
  the report instead.
- A simplification must not change what a test can catch. Where you removed an
  assertion, name the assertion that implies it.

Report:
- Before and after: tests, assertions, lines.
- Deleted tests, grouped by reason. For each, the surviving cover, or the one-line
  reason it was not worth keeping.
- Merges and simplifications: what went into what, and the lines each file lost.
- Notable keeps: tests you considered deleting but kept, and why.
- Plants, and which test caught each.
- Tests outside tools/story-mcp/test that your deletions rely on.
- Dead code, stale docs or spec text, and gaps (promises with no test). One line each.

If you are unsure whether a promise a caller relies on is still covered, keep the test
and say so. Losing the only guard of a real promise is still the one mistake that matters
more than leaving an extra test in. But being unsure whether a test is worth keeping is
not a reason to keep it. If you cannot say in one line what plausible regression it
catches that a caller would notice, delete it.

title: Unit-test pruning: spec-resource
description:
Apply the exact requested pruning prompt recursively to implementation/spec-resource/test. This is a distinct worker cluster under rf2-0wcq5. Production code remains unchanged except temporary hash-verified fault plants. Push a draft test-only PR, babysit all latest-head checks to green, then mark ready. A measured no-op or unexecuted-file report is valid; do not manufacture changes.

Simplify the unit tests under implementation/spec-resource/test. Do not change the code under test. LLMs tend to
write too many low-value unit tests, and this suite was largely written by them.

Assume the suite has more tests than it needs, and that many of its tests are longer
than they need to be. Every test costs CI time, reading time and refactoring friction,
and the low-value ones hide the tests that matter. I want a lean suite: each test earns
its place by guarding a behaviour a caller relies on, against a regression that could
plausibly happen and would matter. Each surviving test should be as short as the thing
it proves.

Stay inside implementation/spec-resource/test. Do not edit tests elsewhere. If a deletion relies on a test outside
implementation/spec-resource/test to keep covering something, name that test in your report.

Work in this order:
1. Run the suite and record the result: tests, assertions, failures, lines. Confirm a
   runner actually executes each file in implementation/spec-resource/test; a file nothing runs cannot be pruned on
   evidence, so report it.
2. Read the code under test and list what it promises its callers: normal results, each
   boundary that takes its own path, each promised failure, and any past bug the tests
   refer to.
3. Map every test to the promise it checks. Most of the work shows up in this map:
   promises with five tests, tests with no promise, and tests of something no caller
   relies on.
4. Decide each test: keep, simplify, merge or delete.
5. Run the suite again and prove the pruned suite still guards every promise.

Work in small batches by contract group, and commit as you go. Before each batch,
predict the change in test and assertion counts; after it, confirm the counts moved by
exactly that much. If helper agents are available, use read-only ones for the mapping
step. If implementation/spec-resource/test plainly will not finish in about four hours, stop at a group boundary,
ship what is done, and list the files you did not reach.

Decide each test with two questions:
- If this test were deleted, what bug could ship that no remaining test would catch?
  If you cannot name one, delete it.
- If you can name one: is that bug plausible in this code, would a caller notice it,
  and would nothing else surface it at once (a compile or load error, a boot-time
  validation, most of the suite going red)? If the bug is implausible, harmless, or
  loud anyway, delete the test.

Delete:
- A test another test implies. If A cannot pass while B fails, drop B.
- Extra examples of one behaviour that take the same path through the code.
- Existence and smoke checks: a function exists, a var resolves, something "is
  registered", a result is non-nil, a call "does not throw", when another test
  exercises the same call with a real assertion.
- Change detectors: a test that copies a constant, a data table, a default config, a
  roster or a string out of the source and asserts equality. It fails on every intended
  change and catches no bug. The exception is a value callers depend on exactly, such as
  a public id or a documented default, that nothing else pins: keep one test for it.
- Absence checks for things nothing produces, and negative-input tests for inputs no
  caller passes and the contract does not mention.
- Exhaustive enumeration: one row per enum member, keyword or field when they all take
  one path. Keep one representative plus the members that take a different path.
- Tests of the language, a library or the framework: a constructor sets a field, a
  getter returns it, a map holds the key just put in it.
- Tests that pin how the code works instead of what it does: private helpers already
  exercised through the public path, call order, internal data shapes, greps of the
  implementation's own source, and log, trace or error wording that is not part of the
  contract.
- Tests whose expected value is computed by the same logic as the code under test.
- Assertions that a mock returned what it was told to return, and tests whose mock setup
  is most of the test while the assertion checks the mock.
- Separate per-platform test files asserting the same thing about platform-neutral code.
  A single shared test that runs on both platforms is one test, not two: keep it.
- Tests of test helpers and fixtures.
- Tests of code that has no logic in it, and tests whose only subject is production code
  that no production caller uses.

Simplify every test you keep:
- Assert the whole result with one equality instead of one assertion per field. Drop an
  assertion that a later one in the same test implies.
- Cut setup, fixtures and data to what the assertion needs. Remove unused bindings,
  requires, helpers and fixtures.
- Tests that vary one input become one table-driven test. Keep the boundary rows and
  drop the mid-range ones.
- Tests that repeat the same setup for one assertion each become one test.
- Delete comments and docstrings that restate the code or narrate history. Keep a
  one-line why where a test's purpose is not obvious from its name and body.
- Rename a test only when its name no longer says what it asserts, and first check that
  nothing matches on the name, such as a CI filter, a skip list or a doc that cites it.

Keep, however small:
- The only test of a promise a caller relies on: a normal result, a boundary that takes
  a different path (empty, one, many; zero; the limit and one past it), a promised
  failure.
- A regression test for a bug that actually happened, unless a stronger test now covers
  it.
- The last guard of a security, privacy or redaction promise.
- The last test that keeps a gate able to fail, and the last test holding a published
  doc or spec claim to the code.
When a weak test and a strong test overlap, keep the strong one: the one that would fail
on more bugs.

Do not:
- Weaken an assertion, or swap an exact check for a looser one, to make a merge or a
  simplification easier.
- Delete a test because it fails, is slow or is flaky. Report it.
- Leave unused helpers, fixtures or requires behind.
- Add new tests. If you find a promise with no test, report it.
- Change production code. Dead code and stale docs or spec text go in your report as a
  list, not into your change.
If anything pins test counts or names, such as a count floor or a roster, update it in
the same change. Commit one file or module at a time.

Prove it:
- The suite passes before and after. Report both sets of counts.
- For each group of deletions that rests on a surviving cover, break the code in a place
  the deleted tests guarded and confirm a surviving test fails. Then restore the code and
  confirm it matches the committed file. One plant per group sharing a cover is enough.
  If nothing fails, you removed real coverage: put the tests back.
- A cover must actually run. A skipped test, a fixture the runner never loads, or a test
  on a lane nothing executes covers nothing. Confirm the runner executes a cover before
  resting a deletion on it.
- Run each test file you touched on its own at least once. Deleting a file can break a
  sibling that relied on it loading something first; give such a file its own require.
- A deletion made under the second question needs no plant. Give its one-line reason in
  the report instead.
- A simplification must not change what a test can catch. Where you removed an
  assertion, name the assertion that implies it.

Report:
- Before and after: tests, assertions, lines.
- Deleted tests, grouped by reason. For each, the surviving cover, or the one-line
  reason it was not worth keeping.
- Merges and simplifications: what went into what, and the lines each file lost.
- Notable keeps: tests you considered deleting but kept, and why.
- Plants, and which test caught each.
- Tests outside implementation/spec-resource/test that your deletions rely on.
- Dead code, stale docs or spec text, and gaps (promises with no test). One line each.

If you are unsure whether a promise a caller relies on is still covered, keep the test
and say so. Losing the only guard of a real promise is still the one mistake that matters
more than leaving an extra test in. But being unsure whether a test is worth keeping is
not a reason to keep it. If you cannot say in one line what plausible regression it
catches that a caller would notice, delete it.
